claims.text: At stage-1, OrdersController.Get had no [Authorize] and no ownership check, so customer 1 reading order 3 (customer 2's) got 200.
In the donhang realm all five customers have the same realm role customer; order 1 belongs to customer 1 and order 3 to customer 2.
ABAC decides access from attributes of the subject (caller), the object (resource) and the environment/request, rather than from roles alone; a role can be one of those attributes.
claims.source_hint: NIST SP 800-162 (Guide to ABAC) §2; glossary entry abac

claims.text: Program.cs defines the OrderOwner policy with one requirement (AddRequirements(new OrderOwnerRequirement())) and registers OrderOwnerHandler as an IAuthorizationHandler.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Api/Program.cs:62-67; ASP.NET Core docs: Policy-based authorization (requirements, handler registration)

claims.text: [Authorize] attribute evaluation happens before the action runs (before data binding and before the code that loads the resource), so it cannot see the loaded order; resource-based checks call IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync imperatively.
claims.source_hint: refs/aspnetcore-docs/aspnetcore/security/authorization/resource-based.md:17 ('Attribute evaluation occurs before data binding...'); mvc resource-based authorization doc

claims.text: IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(ClaimsPrincipal user, object resource, string policyName) returns an AuthorizationResult whose Succeeded tells whether the policy was met for that resource.

IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync evaluates the named policy's requirements with the registered handlers; AuthorizationHandler<TReq, TResource>.HandleRequirementAsync receives the resource (an Order); Succeed marks it met; a requirement left unmet fails the policy.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Resource-based authorization (Create a resource-based handler); Policy-based authorization ('Handler return values')

claims.text: In OrderOwnerHandler, context.User.IsInRole("staff") is true for the staff token because RoleClaimType = "roles" and the token's roles claim contains staff.
claims.source_hint: API docs: ClaimsPrincipal.IsInRole / ClaimsIdentity.RoleClaimType; Program.cs:55; OrderOwnerHandler.cs:22

claims.text: OrderOwnerHandler: staff succeed; otherwise it reads sub (the caller's Keycloak user id, stored in customers.identity_subject), finds the customer with FindByIdentitySubjectAsync and succeeds only when caller.Id == order.CustomerId.

Get and Cancel: [Authorize] (401 with no valid token), FindForReadingAsync, NotFound() if null, then AuthorizeAsync(User, order, "OrderOwner") and Forbid() when not Succeeded; Cancel does this before CancelOrderAsync.
Forbid() from a controller with an authenticated JwtBearer caller produces 403; a missing token on an [Authorize] endpoint produces a 401 challenge.
order-owner.sh output: customer 1 reads order 1 -> 200, reads order 3 -> 403, cancels order 3 -> 403; staff reads order 3 -> 200; no token -> 401; order 3 afterwards still paid.
The arguments of [Authorize] are names (Policy, Roles, AuthenticationSchemes strings); C# attribute arguments must be compile-time constants, so an attribute cannot receive a loaded order.
claims.source_hint: API docs: AuthorizeAttribute (Policy, Roles, AuthenticationSchemes); C# language spec: attribute parameter types (constant expressions)

claims.text: The order stores its owner in customer_id, so comparing it with the caller needs no new role when a customer signs up and reads the owner from the order on every request; a role per customer would need a new realm role per sign-up.
